title: SPX101 Week 9: Performance Analysis & Applied Testing
description: 45 teacher-approved questions on performance analysis workflows, specificity, measurement quality, upper-body power monitoring, clinical home rehab, sarcopenia screening, and the 4m gait speed protocol.
approvedBy: SPX101 Teaching Team (Static Course Snapshot v1.1.0)

questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: An athlete improves their test result slightly. What should you consider before concluding that performance genuinely improved?

options.text: Whether the change exceeds the test's typical measurement error
Whether the equipment brand is popular among professional clubs
Whether the athlete was listed first on the team testing sheet
Whether the athlete personally prefers this exercise over others

questions.explanation: A small observed change may lie within the test's measurement error (minimum detectable difference) rather than reflecting genuine physiological improvement.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Intro to Performance Analysis

questions.learningOutcome: Structure a repeatable testing workflow from planning through interpretation
questions.stem: Which sequence best represents the four linked stages of applied performance analysis taught in Week 9?

options.text: Observation, measurement, interpretation, and application
Measurement, publication, ranking, and athlete replacement
Purchase equipment, collect big data, store files, and archive
Intuition, isolated testing, raw score reporting, and billing

questions.explanation: Performance analysis links four stages: observing movement/workload, measuring data, interpreting what the data mean in context, and applying findings to guide decisions.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Four-Step Process

questions.learningOutcome: Identify how test purpose changes metric choice, protocol design, and communication strategy
questions.stem: What should always be established before selecting and administering a performance or clinical test?

options.text: A clear sport, clinical, or rehabilitation question to answer
Access to the most expensive laboratory sensor system available
Confirmation that every other team in the league runs the test
A target for collecting the largest possible spreadsheet of numbers

questions.explanation: Testing should never be done merely because a tool is available; it must begin with a meaningful question whose answer will inform a practical decision.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Purpose First

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the principle of specificity when deciding whether a test is useful
questions.stem: Why is a submaximal cycling test of limited practical value for evaluating a competitive basketball player's court fitness?

options.text: It lacks movement and task specificity for basketball court demands
Cycling makes it impossible to record heart rate during exercise
Cycle ergometers cannot be operated inside an indoor sports hall
Basketball players are prohibited from using stationary ergometers

questions.explanation: While a cycling test gives a general indicator of aerobic fitness, it does not reflect the intermittent running, jumping, and directional demands of basketball.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Specificity Matters

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the principle of specificity when deciding whether a test is useful
questions.stem: For a rugby league prop forward, why is a 15-metre sprint assessment typically more informative than a 100-metre sprint test?

options.text: Props rarely sprint 100 m in matches, whereas short acceleration matters
Timing gates cannot measure distances longer than 20 metres accurately
A 15-metre sprint measures maximal aerobic capacity better than 100 m
Rugby league pitches are only 15 metres long from try-line to try-line

questions.explanation: Specificity requires matching the test to the actual positional role demands: props rely on short-range acceleration and contact tolerance rather than 100-metre sprinting.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Specificity Matters

questions.learningOutcome: Recognise why test results should be interpreted in context
questions.stem: What lesson does Kevin Durant's inability to complete the NBA Combine bench press test illustrate about athlete testing?

options.text: A poor score on a non-specific test may not limit actual sport success
Upper-body strength testing is always harmful for basketball players
Basketball performance depends entirely on maximal bench press load
Physical testing alone guarantees which draftees will become stars

questions.explanation: Not every isolated test weakness needs fixing if the test lacks specificity to how the athlete actually succeeds in their sporting role.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Specificity and Individual Profiles

questions.learningOutcome: Use validity, reliability, sensitivity, feasibility, and ecological validity to judge test quality
questions.stem: In the context of evaluating an athlete test, what core question does validity ask?

options.text: Does the test actually measure the quality it claims to measure?
Does the test give identical numbers when repeated ten minutes later?
Can the test be purchased without a recurring software subscription?
Can an entire squad complete the test in less than fifteen minutes?

questions.explanation: Validity asks whether a test genuinely measures what it claims to measure for the target population and context.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Measurement Quality

questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: A patient walks at 1.00 m/s on a gait test with a minimum detectable difference of 0.10 m/s. Next month they record 1.05 m/s. How should you interpret this?

options.text: We cannot be confident of real improvement as 0.05 m/s is within error
The patient has definitively improved walking speed by five percent
The timing equipment must have malfunctioned during the second trial
The patient should immediately stop rehabilitation as goals are met

questions.explanation: Because the 0.05 m/s change is smaller than the 0.10 m/s minimum detectable difference (measurement error), we cannot distinguish the change from noise.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Sensitivity and Measurement Error

questions.learningOutcome: Use validity, reliability, sensitivity, feasibility, and ecological validity to judge test quality
questions.stem: Why should hospitals and sports clubs evaluate vendor lock-in and cloud database reliance when assessing test feasibility?

options.text: Policy changes or company failure can render historical data inaccessible
Cloud databases physically increase the weight of force plate sensors
Digital uploads automatically invalidate criterion validity statistics
Subscription software prevents load cells from ever needing calibration

questions.explanation: Feasibility includes long-term sustainability: if a third-party cloud vendor shuts down or hospital IT blocks external database access, the tool and past data can be lost.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Feasibility in Real-World Settings

questions.learningOutcome: Distinguish meaningful signals from normal variation in sport environments
questions.stem: Why can a simple, feasible field test repeated weekly often be more useful for athlete management than a highly precise lab test done twice a year?

options.text: Frequent longitudinal data support timely, actionable training adjustments
Simple field tests have zero random or systematic measurement error
Laboratory metabolic carts cannot measure oxygen consumption accurately
Twice-yearly testing is prohibited under professional sports regulations

questions.explanation: More accurate does not always mean more useful; regular weekly monitoring captures trends over time that practitioners can actually act upon during a season.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Ease of Implementation vs Accuracy

questions.topic: Sensitivity to Change in Gym Testing
questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: An athlete's single-leg hamstring curl 1RM is 20 kg, and the next pin increment on the machine is 22.5 kg. Why is this a sensitivity problem?

options.text: A 12.5% strength gain is required before the score can change at all
Cable weight stacks only measure eccentric force rather than concentric
Single-leg tests cannot be performed safely on pin-loaded gym machines
Weight stacks automatically adjust resistance to keep velocity constant

questions.explanation: Jumping from 20 kg to 22.5 kg requires a 12.5% improvement; smaller but meaningful strength gains will be missed completely, which can demotivate the athlete or patient.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Sensitivity to Change in Training

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the idea of practical alternatives when specialised equipment is not available
questions.stem: When a pin-loaded machine has coarse weight increments (e.g., 2.5 kg jumps), which strategy can improve sensitivity to detect progress?

options.text: Measure lever-arm velocity with an IMU, use a load cell, or add micro-plates
Estimate the athlete's improvement visually without recording numbers
Wait two years between tests so the strength gain exceeds 50 percent
Round every recorded lift up to the nearest 10-kilogram increment

questions.explanation: Adding fractional 500 g plates, inline load cells, or measuring peak angular velocity of the lever arm with a phone IMU detects power/strength gains at the same load.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Sensitivity Solutions

questions.learningOutcome: Use validity, reliability, sensitivity, feasibility, and ecological validity to judge test quality
questions.stem: What does ecological validity refer to when comparing a laboratory test with a field-based sports assessment?

options.text: How well the test environment and task reflect real-world competition demands
Whether the testing equipment is manufactured from recyclable materials
How long the wireless sensor batteries last during outdoor sessions
Whether the laboratory air conditioning stays at an exact temperature

questions.explanation: Ecological validity describes how closely a test reflects what actually happens in the person's real-world sporting or daily environment.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Field vs Laboratory Tests

questions.learningOutcome: Communicate findings with appropriate caution, limitations, and action-focused recommendations
questions.stem: A player's monitoring battery indicates elevated fatigue and asymmetry. How should a sports scientist communicate this to the head coach?

options.text: Explain that indicators suggest higher injury risk and discuss load options
Guarantee that the player will tear a muscle if they play this weekend
Withhold the data because fatigue tests have zero relationship to injury
Unilaterally bench the player and override the coaching and medical staff

questions.explanation: Testing identifies risk indicators rather than certainties; practitioners should communicate elevated risk and recovery options clearly so coaches can make informed decisions.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Injury Prevention and Management

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret monitoring data in relation to training load, readiness, and adaptation goals
questions.stem: How has modern evidence-based return-to-sport practice improved upon traditional fixed-time recovery rules (e.g., 'wait six weeks')?

options.text: Progression is guided by meeting functional and strength benchmarks
All athletes now return in exactly half the calendar time regardless of pain
Players only return once they achieve a personal best 100 m sprint time
Injured athletes avoid all physical movement until match day arrives

questions.explanation: Modern return-to-sport uses objective functional thresholds, strength restoration, and symptom-free sport-specific progression rather than arbitrary calendar timelines alone.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Return to Sport Benchmarks

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret monitoring data in relation to training load, readiness, and adaptation goals
questions.stem: Why do sports scientists combine internal load (e.g., heart rate), external load (e.g., GPS distance/impacts), and performance tests when monitoring fatigue?

options.text: No single metric captures fatigue completely without broader context
External GPS load measures heart rate variability more directly than ECG
Combining three metrics eliminates the need to speak with the athlete
Internal load only changes when an athlete is completely dehydrated

questions.explanation: As highlighted by Halson's monitoring framework, no single measure perfectly captures fatigue; combining internal load, external load, and performance context prevents misinterpretation.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Monitoring Fatigue and Adaptation

questions.learningOutcome: Use monitoring outputs to support practical training decisions rather than data overload
questions.stem: Which three core questions must an effective practitioner be able to answer clearly about any test they run?

options.text: What do we measure, what does it mean, and what do we do about it?
Who built the sensor, what is the patent number, and how much did it cost?
Which algorithm was used, how many lines of code, and what is the R-squared?
Who came first, who came last, and how can we punish the slowest player?

questions.explanation: Complex algorithms are useless if they cannot guide action; a practitioner must clearly explain what is measured, what it means, and what practical action follows.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Turning Data into Decisions

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why a common strength test, such as the bench press 1RM, may not fully capture sport-specific power demands
questions.stem: In a standard heavy bench press, where in the range of motion is peak force typically produced, and why does this limit specificity for grappling/palming off?

options.text: Near the chest early in the lift, whereas sport demands high force near extension
At full elbow lockout, whereas sport only requires force at the chest
Force is identical at every millimetre, so velocity never changes in sport
Only during the pause on the chest, where tendons cannot store energy

questions.explanation: In a traditional bench press, peak force occurs early right after the chest counter-movement and drops to ~50% near terminal extension, whereas fending/grappling requires high force and power toward extended elbow positions.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Sports Performance Monitoring and Upper-Body Power

questions.learningOutcome: Describe how force, velocity, range of motion, and movement specificity influence power testing
questions.stem: Why is a ballistic bench throw used instead of a standard bench press when assessing explosive upper-body power?

options.text: It allows continuous acceleration throughout the range rather than decelerating
It allows the athlete to lift a heavier 1RM load than a standard bench press
It eliminates the need for any safety equipment or braking mechanism
It forces the barbell to move at a slow, constant isometric velocity

questions.explanation: In a standard bench press, the lifter must decelerate the bar to stop at full elbow extension; a bench throw propels the bar to emphasize velocity and power right through terminal extension.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Bench Throw Power

questions.learningOutcome: Recognise why safety and impact reduction are essential when designing explosive testing and training tasks
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of an electromagnetic brake on a Smith machine during heavy bench throws or jump squats?

options.text: To control or arrest the descending barbell and reduce catching impact risk
To push the barbell upward so the athlete achieves a higher jump score
To measure blood lactate concentration directly through the barbell grip
To lock the barbell before the athlete begins the upward concentric push

questions.explanation: Safety is paramount in explosive testing; an electromagnetic brake slows or stops the descending load so athletes are not injured trying to catch heavy falling loads.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Safety and Braking Systems

questions.learningOutcome: Describe how force, velocity, range of motion, and movement specificity influence power testing
questions.stem: In the Week 9 Smith-machine bench throw setup, how were power and range-of-motion data calculated?

options.text: Combining force from a plate under the bench with displacement/velocity from a linear transducer
Timing the lift with a handheld stopwatch and multiplying by body mass
Recording surface EMG voltage alone and converting millivolts directly into watts
Measuring peak heart rate after the throw and dividing by barbell weight

questions.explanation: A force plate under the bench directly measured force while a linear position transducer (string potentiometer) sampled barbell displacement over time to derive velocity and power.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Force Plate and Linear Transducer

questions.learningOutcome: Compare static-start and counter-movement bench throw approaches for assessing explosive upper-body power
questions.stem: Why does a half-range counter-movement bench throw typically produce greater throw height and force than a static-start throw from the same midpoint?

options.text: Muscles and tendons store and recoil elastic energy during the counter-movement
The barbell travels zero vertical distance during a counter-movement throw
Gravity is temporarily eliminated when the linear transducer beeps
The electromagnetic brake reduces barbell mass during the upward push

questions.explanation: The dynamic counter-movement utilizes the stretch-shortening cycle, storing elastic energy in tendons and muscles to generate higher force and throw height than a static start.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Static vs Counter-Movement Throws

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the idea of practical alternatives when specialised equipment is not available
questions.stem: When an electromagnetic brake is unavailable, how can a coach assess or train explosive lower-body power while minimizing landing joint impact?

options.text: Jump onto an elevated bench/box or perform a single-leg press to a double-leg catch
Perform maximal depth jumps onto concrete while holding heavy dumbbells
Land with fully locked knees and hips to absorb force through bone alone
Have athletes jump blindfolded so they do not tense before ground contact

questions.explanation: Jumping onto a bench reduces vertical drop distance and landing velocity, while a single-leg press with a two-leg catch distributes landing force across both limbs to reduce knee impact.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Practical Alternatives and Impact Reduction

questions.learningOutcome: Explain how performance monitoring can be applied to clinical populations and home-based rehabilitation
questions.stem: In the 2024 Singapore total knee arthroplasty (TKA) home-rehab study, why were Bluetooth and wall-mounted LiDAR used instead of Wi-Fi video cameras?

options.text: To protect in-home patient privacy and security while passively tracking gait speed
Because video cameras cannot record human walking indoors under artificial light
Because Singapore hospitals had not yet invented wireless internet routers
Because wall-mounted LiDAR takes daily X-rays of the metallic knee implant

questions.explanation: Patient privacy, cybersecurity concerns, and multilingual usability ruled out in-home cloud video cameras and complex text prompts; Bluetooth sensors and wall-mounted LiDAR provided passive, private daily monitoring.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Clinical Performance Monitoring

questions.learningOutcome: Describe how technologies such as LIDAR, digital goniometers, and modified bathroom scales can support practical clinical assessment
questions.stem: In the TKA home rehabilitation system, what clinical issue did the wireless modified bathroom scales specifically monitor and help retrain during sit-to-stands?

options.text: Limb weight-bearing asymmetry as patients avoided loading the operated leg
Maximal oxygen uptake during high-intensity treadmill running intervals
Hand grip strength asymmetry following upper-limb shoulder surgery
Femoral bone mineral density changes measured via X-ray attenuation

questions.explanation: After total knee replacement, patients naturally offload the operated leg; dual wireless bathroom scales acting as force plates tracked left-right weight asymmetry and guided progressive symmetrical loading.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Modified Bathroom Scales in Home Rehab

questions.learningOutcome: Recognise why co-design with clinicians, patients, athletes, and end users is essential for real-world implementation
questions.stem: Why did the TKA home-rehab interface use blue-and-yellow visual demonstrations and large squishy goniometer handles?

options.text: Co-design addressed colour-vision accessibility, language barriers, and grip limitations
Blue and yellow were required by the equipment manufacturer's trademark law
Blue pixels consume zero tablet battery power during Bluetooth transmission
Squishy handles make the digital goniometer sample joint angles ten times faster

questions.explanation: Co-designing with clinicians and patients led to easy-grip handles for older hands, visual/video guidance across languages, and a blue-yellow palette optimal for colour-blind accessibility.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Co-Design with End Users

questions.learningOutcome: Explain how performance monitoring can be applied to clinical populations and home-based rehabilitation
questions.stem: What did the 'non-inferiority' finding of the home-based TKA monitoring study demonstrate compared with traditional hospital physiotherapy?

options.text: Home-based monitored rehab achieved clinical outcomes no worse than hospital care
Home-based rehab produced significantly worse knee flexion than no rehab at all
Hospital physiotherapy should be banned for all orthopaedic surgical patients
Surgery itself is unnecessary when patients own a pair of bathroom scales

questions.explanation: A non-inferiority design tests whether a more scalable, lower-cost home intervention achieves outcomes that are at least comparable (not clinically inferior) to standard hospital care.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Non-Inferiority Outcomes

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why automated grip strength, gait speed, and body composition testing may improve sarcopenia screening
questions.stem: How is sarcopenia defined in the clinical performance monitoring module, and which measures are central to rapid screening?

options.text: Age-related loss of muscle mass plus low muscle strength or poor physical performance
Age-related loss of bone calcium diagnosed solely through maximal sprint cycling
Acute ligament rupture in youth athletes assessed via counter-movement bench throws
Decline in forced expiratory lung volume measured during underwater weighing

questions.explanation: Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass combined with low muscle strength (e.g., grip strength) and/or poor physical performance (e.g., gait speed).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Diagnosing Sarcopenia in the Real World

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why automated grip strength, gait speed, and body composition testing may improve sarcopenia screening
questions.stem: In diagnostic screening for sarcopenia, what is the difference between diagnostic sensitivity and diagnostic specificity?

options.text: Sensitivity correctly identifies those with sarcopenia; specificity correctly identifies those without it
Sensitivity measures sensor sampling rate; specificity measures battery voltage stability
Both terms mean the exact same thing as test-retest correlation across days
A sensitivity of 0.50 means the screening test is ninety-five percent accurate

questions.explanation: In diagnostic testing, high sensitivity (e.g., 0.95) means few true cases are missed, whereas high specificity means healthy individuals are rarely misdiagnosed as having the condition.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Optimizing Sarcopenia Screening

questions.learningOutcome: Explain why automated grip strength, gait speed, and body composition testing may improve sarcopenia screening
questions.stem: How does combining automated LiDAR gait speed, digital grip strength, and bioimpedance scales improve real-world sarcopenia screening?

options.text: It completes screening in under a minute while cutting manual timing error and setup time
It replaces the need for patients to ever walk or squeeze a handle during testing
It performs an automated muscle biopsy during the four-metre walking trial
It guarantees that every older adult will be classified as having severe sarcopenia

questions.explanation: Integrating automated LiDAR gait speed, grip dynamometry, and bioimpedance removes manual tape-measure/stopwatch errors and reduces screening time and error by roughly tenfold.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Automated Sarcopenia Screening

questions.learningOutcome: Structure a repeatable testing workflow from planning through interpretation
questions.stem: In the SPX101 8-metre track setup for the 4-metre walk test, how are the four floor lines arranged and which section is timed?

options.text: 0–2 m acceleration, 2–6 m timed 4 m zone, and 6–8 m deceleration zone
0–4 m timed from a standing start, followed by a 4–8 m cool-down walk
All 8 metres are timed and the final stopwatch reading is divided by two
0–3 m acceleration, 3–5 m timed 2 m zone, and 5–8 m deceleration zone

questions.explanation: The track uses lines at 0 m, 2 m, 6 m, and 8 m: a 2 m acceleration zone, a middle 4 m timed section (between 2 m and 6 m), and a 2 m deceleration zone.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: During the 4-metre walk test, why should the assessor NOT draw the participant's attention to the 2-metre and 6-metre timing lines?

options.text: Participants may look down and alter their natural step pattern to target the lines
Participants are required to keep their eyes closed throughout the entire walk
Knowing where the lines are causes the stopwatch to run at double speed
Looking at painted floor lines always causes healthy adults to lose balance

questions.explanation: Drawing attention to the middle timing lines encourages participants to look down or take an unnatural stride to cross the line, distorting their natural walking speed.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: Where should the assessor position themselves while walking with the participant during the 4-metre gait speed test, and why?

options.text: Slightly behind and to the side so the participant does not pace off the tester
Directly in front walking backward to maintain eye contact with the participant
Shoulder-to-shoulder at a brisk march to encourage a faster walking cadence
Twenty metres away in another room to avoid influencing the environment

questions.explanation: Walking slightly behind and to the side keeps the tester close enough to assist safely without causing the participant to unconsciously match the tester's stride or cadence.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Structure a repeatable testing workflow from planning through interpretation
questions.stem: In the SPX101 4-metre walk test protocol, what exact event triggers starting and stopping the stopwatch at the 2 m and 6 m lines?

options.text: When either foot (typically the leading toes) first crosses the respective line
Only when the participant'sboth heels have completely cleared the line
When the top of the participant's head passes above the painted floor mark
When the participant shouts 'start' at 2 m and 'stop' at the 6 m mark

questions.explanation: The timer starts when either foot (usually the toes) first crosses the 2-metre line and stops when either foot first crosses the 6-metre line.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Apply quality checks that improve confidence in observed changes over time
questions.stem: Why can two normal walking trials by the same person differ in stopwatch time simply because of where their foot lands near the timing line?

options.text: Landing just before the line can require almost an entire extra gait cycle to cross
Indoor floor friction doubles whenever a shoe touches painted line tape
Smartphone timers reset to zero whenever a step lands near a line
Walking four metres causes severe muscular acidosis by the second trial

questions.explanation: If a foot lands just short of the timing line, the participant needs nearly an extra step/gait cycle before a foot crosses the line, creating trial-to-trial variability and motivating multiple trials.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret physical activity and performance data in ways that support appropriate program planning
questions.stem: If a participant completes the 4-metre timed walking zone in 3.20 seconds, what is their calculated gait speed in metres per second (m/s)?

options.text: 1.25 m/s (4.0 metres divided by 3.20 seconds)
0.80 m/s (3.20 seconds divided by 4.0 metres)
2.50 m/s (8.0 total track metres divided by 3.20 seconds)
12.80 m/s (4.0 metres multiplied by 3.20 seconds)

questions.explanation: Speed equals timed distance divided by time: 4.0 m / 3.20 s = 1.25 m/s (using the 4 m timed zone, not the 8 m total track length).
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Communicate findings with appropriate caution, limitations, and action-focused recommendations
questions.stem: Why is a manual stopwatch error of ±0.10 m/s problematic when screening an older adult near the 0.80 m/s frailty/sarcopenia gait speed cut-point?

options.text: Normal measurement noise can flip the patient above (0.85) or below (0.75) the threshold
Anyone walking 0.80 m/s is moving too fast for a human eye to see
Stopwatches record speed in kilometres per hour rather than seconds
Clinical cut-points are unaffected by random or systematic timing errors

questions.explanation: When measurement error (±0.10 m/s) is large relative to a clinical decision threshold (0.80 m/s), the same person can be classified as healthy one day and at-risk the next purely due to noise.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 4 & Week 9 Part 3: Clinical Cut-Points

questions.learningOutcome: Interpret monitoring data in relation to training load, readiness, and adaptation goals
questions.stem: A soccer midfielder shows a drop in repeated-sprint output late in matches. According to Week 9, how should an analyst approach this finding?

options.text: Investigate multiple contextual explanations such as aerobic fitness, recovery, tactics, or role load
Immediately conclude the player has poor maximal 1RM bench press strength
Ignore the data because late-match fatigue is purely psychological
Release the player from the squad without checking training or match context

questions.explanation: Observation and measurement require contextual interpretation: late-match sprint decline could reflect aerobic conditioning, between-effort recovery, tactical demands, muscle fatigue, or pacing.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Observation to Interpretation

questions.learningOutcome: Structure a repeatable testing workflow from planning through interpretation
questions.stem: If a proposed athlete test is valid, reliable, and sensitive, why might a sports scientist still decide NOT to include it in the team's testing battery?

options.text: If the results will not actually change training, rehab, or coaching practice
Because valid and reliable tests are always too inexpensive to look impressive
Because coaches prefer tests that have high random error and low repeatability
Because any test that takes under five minutes is scientifically invalid

questions.explanation: The final test-selection filter is practical utility: 'Will it change practice?' Collecting data that no one acts upon wastes athlete and staff time.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 1: Practical Framework for Selecting a Test

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the idea of practical alternatives when specialised equipment is not available
questions.stem: Which bodyweight exercise is highlighted in Week 9 as a feasible, lower-risk alternative to barbell bench throws for upper-body explosive power?

options.text: Controlled push-up jumps where no external barbell needs to be caught
Sixty-second isometric abdominal planks held on an unstable foam mat
Slow seated dumbbell wrist curls performed to muscular exhaustion
Maximal barbell shoulder shrugs held for ten seconds at the top

questions.explanation: Push-up jumps assess and train explosive upper-body extension without the risk of catching a falling loaded barbell when braking equipment is unavailable.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Practical Alternatives

questions.learningOutcome: Use validity, reliability, sensitivity, feasibility, and ecological validity to judge test quality
questions.stem: In the laboratory validation of the low-cost LiDAR speed sensor, what gold-standard criterion reference was it compared against?

options.text: A 3D optical motion analysis camera system tracking reflective markers
A single novice assessor clicking a mechanical handheld stopwatch
A mechanical waist-mounted step-counter pedometer from a pharmacy
Participants' subjective rating of how fast they felt they were walking

questions.explanation: Criterion validity was established by comparing LiDAR velocity profiles directly against a laboratory 3D motion-capture camera system.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2 & Week 9 Part 3: LiDAR Validation

questions.learningOutcome: Describe how technologies such as LIDAR, digital goniometers, and modified bathroom scales can support practical clinical assessment
questions.stem: What advantage does high-frequency LiDAR tracking offer over standard timing gates set at 0 m, 10 m, and 20 m?

options.text: It captures the continuous acceleration trajectory between points, not just split times
It eliminates air resistance for the sprinter during outdoor 100 m races
It automatically adjusts the athlete's footwear traction during changes of direction
It directly measures arterial blood oxygen saturation from across the field

questions.explanation: Timing gates only provide discrete split times at gate locations, whereas high-frequency LiDAR samples distance continuously to reveal the full acceleration and velocity curve.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W05-P450] Week 5 Part 2 & Week 9 Part 3: LiDAR Field Assessments

questions.topic: Participant Safety Instructions in Gait Testing
questions.learningOutcome: Adapts monitoring principles to clinical populations with safety and context in mind
questions.stem: What explicit safety instruction is given to the participant before starting the 4-metre walk test in the Week 9 demonstration?

options.text: Walk at normal speed, and stop immediately and tell the tester if feeling worried, unsteady, or dizzy
Run as fast as humanly possible and dive across the final 8-metre line
Continue walking even if dizzy so the trial timer does not have to be reset
Walk backward through the deceleration zone to test vestibular balance

questions.explanation: Participants are instructed to walk at their natural shopping-corridor pace and to stop straight away and notify the tester if they feel worried, might slip, or feel dizzy.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P474] Week 9.3 Mastery Assessment Workshop 2 - Gait Speed

questions.learningOutcome: Compare static-start and counter-movement bench throw approaches for assessing explosive upper-body power
questions.stem: In the half-range counter-movement bench throw video, how did the system standardize the depth at which the front-rower reversed the barbell?

options.text: The linear transducer triggered an audible beep when the bar reached half range of motion
A wooden block was strapped to the athlete's chest to physically bounce the bar
The athlete guessed the midpoint with their eyes closed on each repetition
A wall clock chimed every five seconds regardless of where the barbell was

questions.explanation: The linear position transducer was programmed to each athlete's individual half-range of motion and emitted a real-time audio beep cueing them to reverse and throw.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 2: Real-Time Feedback in Bench Throws

questions.learningOutcome: Apply the broader lesson that useful technology must be accurate, feasible, interpretable, and connected to better decisions
questions.stem: How can modern camera-based 2D pose tracking address clinical home-privacy concerns that previously blocked video use in patients' homes?

options.text: By processing joint angles locally on the device so raw video is never transmitted
By uploading raw home video to public servers without patient identifiers
By turning off the camera lens and guessing joint angles from room audio
By recording patients only while they are asleep in total darkness

questions.explanation: On-device (local edge) processing extracts skeletal joint angles locally without storing or sending raw video footage anywhere, preserving patient privacy.
questions.sourceRef: [CANVAS-W09-P470] Week 9 Part 3: Future Improvements in Home Monitoring
